SOURCE BLOCK:
"Who hath lain alone to hear the wild goose cry?"

A BOUT once in so often you are due to lie awake at night. Why this is so I have never been able to discover. It apparently comes from no predisposing uneasiness of indigestion, no rashness in the matter of too much tea or tobacco, no excitation of unusual incident or stimulating conversation. In fact, you turn in with the expectation of rather a good night's rest. Almost at once the little noises of the forest grow larger, blend in the hollow bigness of the first drowse; your thoughts drift idly back and forth between reality and dream; when— snap! —you are broad awake!

Perhaps the reservoir of your vital forces is full to the overflow of a little waste; or perhaps, more subtly, the great Mother insists thus that you enter the temple of her larger mysteries.

For, unlike mere insomnia, lying awake at night in the woods is pleasant. The eager, nervous straining for sleep gives way to a delicious indifference. You do not care. Your mind is cradled in an exquisite poppy-suspension of judgment and of thought. Impressions slip vaguely into your consciousness and as vaguely out again. Sometimes they stand stark and naked for your inspection; sometimes they lose themselves in the mist of half-sleep. Always they lay soft velvet fingers on the drowsy imagination, so that in their caressing you feel the vaster spaces from which they have come. Peaceful-brooding your faculties receive. Hearing, sight, smell—all are preternaturally keen to whatever of sound and sight and woods perfume is abroad through the night; and yet at the same time active appreciation dozes, so these things lie on it sweet and cloying like fallen rose-leaves.

In such circumstance you will hear what the voyageurs call the voices of the rapids. Many people never hear them at all. They speak very soft and low and distinct beneath the steady roar and dashing, beneath even the lesser tinklings and gurglings whose quality superimposes them over the louder sounds. They are like the tear-forms swimming across the field of vision, which disappear so quickly when you concentrate your sight to look at them, and which reappear so magically when again your gaze turns vacant. In the stillness of your hazy half-consciousness they speak; when you bend your attention to listen, they are gone, and only the tumults and the tinklings remain.

message.content:
"Who has spent the night alone to hear the wild goose call?"

Occasionally, there comes a moment when you find yourself awake in the stillness of the night. The reason behind this phenomenon eludes me, as it seems unrelated to any discomfort from overindulgence in food, an excess of caffeine, or the excitement of an eventful day. You typically settle in with the hope of enjoying a restful night. Yet, almost instantly, the subtle sounds of the forest amplify, merging into the expansive hush that accompanies the onset of sleep; suddenly—snap!—you find yourself fully alert.

It could be that your reservoir of energy is brimming, or perhaps, more intriguingly, the great Mother calls you forth to explore the deeper mysteries of her domain.

Unlike typical insomnia, being awake at night in the woods has its own charm. The frantic desire to fall asleep fades into a state of blissful apathy. You begin to care less about the need for rest. Your thoughts float in a dreamy suspension, where judgment and reflection are softened. Sensory impressions drift in and out of your awareness. Occasionally, they present themselves clearly for contemplation, while at other times, they dissolve into the haze of near-sleep. They gently caress the drowsy imagination, allowing you to sense the vastness from which they emerge. Your faculties receive this serene ambiance. The senses of hearing, sight, and smell become extraordinarily acute to the sounds and scents that dance through the night air, yet your ability to actively appreciate these sensations drifts into a peaceful slumber, as if they were delicate rose petals.

In these moments, you might hear what the voyageurs refer to as the voices of the rapids. Remarkably, many people go their entire lives without perceiving them. They emerge softly, distinctly beneath the tumultuous sounds of rushing water, even amid the lighter gurgles and tinklings that often overshadow them. They resemble fleeting images that flit across your field of vision, vanishing the instant you focus your gaze, only to reappear enchantingly when you allow your mind to wander again. In that tranquil state of hazy awareness, the voices emerge; yet, when you attempt to listen closely, they recede, leaving only the boisterous cascades and gentle murmurs behind.
